newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish parliament slams security service in vote.
newsitem.headline: Polish parliament slams security service in vote.

text.p: Poland's parliament on Thursday approved a report that said the country's security service acted unlawfully while investigating former Prime Minister Jozef Oleksy on suspicion he informed for Moscow intelligence.

The parliament, dominated by Oleksy's ruling ex-communists, voted by 243 to 90 with 31 abstentions to accept a report by a special committee investigating the service's role in the episode, which led Oleksy to quit as premier in January.
It rejected a dissenting verdict by the minority of opposition parliamentarians on the committee, which merely pointed to shortcomings in the security service operation.

The affair erupted a year ago when then interior minister Andrzej Milczanowski told an astonished parliament that the State Protection Office (UOP) had evidence Oleksy passed information to Soviet and Russian intelligence officers.

Oleksy, while proclaiming his innocence, quit after prosecutors decided to probe the allegations. He now heads the core party in the Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) -- the larger grouping in the ruling coalition.
Prosecutors later dropped their investigation, saying the security service evidence was flawed and inadequate. Thursday's vote was presented by Oleksy's party as a further vindication.
But some opposition politicians disagree, charging that the SLD's current political clout in parliament and government have made a fair assessment of the case impossible.

Oleksy's SLD switched to the attack after the vote, saying it would start proceedings to try Milczanowski -- now a provincial notary -- before a special court for high officials called the State Tribunal.

Ex-communists say the allegations were cooked up by UOP officers sympathetic to former Solidarity leader Lech Walesa, who last December was readying to hand over Poland's presidency to Oleksy's colleague Aleksander Kwasniewski.

"The law must prevent the use of the special services in political actions aimed against that which has been decided by democracy...that is the basic moral of the so-called Oleksy case for Poland and for democracy," President Kwasniewski told a news conference on Thursday.
SLD spokesman Andrzej Urbanczak said his party accused Milczanowski of breaking the law, causing a crisis in the state and using the security service for political ends, PAP news agency reported.
Walesa told the agency that the Solidarity-rooted opposition would get back into power after parliamentary elections next year and would then try some ex-communists.
"When chances are evened up next year, we will have to put many in the SLD before the Tribunal. And we will," he said.

"They have taught us how victors should behave," he added when asked to comment on the SLD decision to try his political ally Milczanowski who quit the interior ministry when Walesa stood down as president in December.
